Coronary artery stents1,42 were initially developed to treat or prevent acute occlusion of the vessel due to elastic recoil after balloon angioplasty, but are now used routinely in most PCI to reduce the risk of restenosis (see below), al- though their effect on mortality is unclear.43 Thrombotic occlusion 2 to 14 days after the procedure (subacute stent thrombosis) is a major complication with stent use, and in- itially led to the use of intensive anticoagulant/antiplatelet regimens.42 However, with optimal stent deployment and use of heparin during the procedure, oral antiplatelet drugs alone appear to be adequate, and a combination of aspirin with clopidogrel is now recommended. Aspirin should be continued indefinitely, but the optimum duration for clopi- dogrel therapy is less clear. For patients with bare metal stents, clopidogrel should be given for at least 2 to 4 weeks,2 and treatment for 12 months has been recom- mended.3,19 For patients with drug-eluting stents, the risk of occlusion persists for longer, and the benefit of continu- ing clopidogrel is better established.44,45 Combination therapy is therefore recommended for at least 12 months,3,19,46 and may be continued indefinitely if tolerat- ed.19 Cilostazol has also been used, both as an alternative to thienopyridines,47,48 and as part of a triple platelet regi- men.49 Heparin-coated stents may also have a role.50 Restenosis is a specific long-term complication of percu- taneous procedures.1,51,52 Several pathological processes are believed to be responsible, including platelet aggrega- tion and thrombus formation, elastic recoil, vascular re- modelling, and neointimal hyperplasia. Symptomatic rest- enosis often requires a repeat revascularisation procedure and increases the risk for clinical events. Stents reduce res- tenosis by preventing elastic recoil and vascular remodel- ling, but are associated with a higher risk of neointimal hyperplasia, and in-stent restenosis is a particular prob- lem.53,54 This has led to the investigation of drugs to pre- vent restenosis, but results have generally been disappoint- ing. Greater success has been reported with drug-eluting stents, and these are now widely used, as discussed below; however, they are not without complications, and oral therapies continue to be investigated. Although systemic therapy with antiplatelet drugs and anticoagulants reduces the risk of thrombus formation, there is little evidence that they reduce the degree of reste- nosis; studies with cilostazol have suggested that it may have some effect,55,56 but this is not yet established.
